So today I have decided that I am going to start exploring non-systemd alternatives. Right now the obvious move for me, a longtime Debian guy, is to go to something like LMDE 2 under sysvinit. I know Debian is stable, and I need it to be for what I am doing with my system.

But then I came across an interesting Manjaro Experiment that I found very interesting and compelling, leading me to now consider Manjaro OpenRC 0.8.13 as a possible alternative. I have spent quite a bit of time with the upcoming Manjaro KDENext distributions so I am pretty comfortable with Manjaro as both an OS and complimentary support and documentation resource.

I know this is just a start, but I wanted to share some of the more interesting and technical information on what, exactly an init system does and how it interacts with your computer. Like most Linux users here I am not merely satisfied with "it just works" I like to dig into the "how's and why's" of things once I decide to look into something. I also have to admit that I do not know as much about init systems as I would like, so I am going to take this opportunity to turn this switch away from systemd into a self-study crash course in the init system topic overall.

As this process of me making the switch away from systemd unfolds I will try and post some of the more interesting and informative stuff I learn and come across during the change over. right now I still have a Windows drive that I can boot into (yes I still have Windows), but I am going to take this opportunity of switching out of systemd to set up my alternate and eventually permanent setup on the SSD Windows currently occupies. I have never had Linux on the SSD, Debian is just as snappy on the 1 TB platter drive as Windows is on the SSD, so I am looking forward to seeing how Linux boots and runs on an SSD.

Right now I am not sure how suitable Manjaro will be for a system that needs to be up, running and stable 24/7 for a Tor relay and i2p hub. I know Debian to be rock solid, in fact I have not even used anything else on my system and do not know how well other OS/Distros will perform for this use. (As a main system, not counting playing with other distros in a VM)

Is there even a real viable option other than a Debian-based distro for the stability and performance I require?

I definitely welcome any and all opinions and thoughts on this subject as I move forward, any interesting articles and links I welcome for sure. I never was into the initial systemd debate, so I do not know all the issues that people were debating, but I do know that it seems to be aggressively taking over a lot of the distros as a default black-box init system, almost out of nowhere. With all the current privacy and spying issues I find this to be concerning. especially given the nature of what I use my system for.
My search for a permanent switch away from systemd begins - Manjaro OpenRC 0.8.13 - reinventing init without systemd

I don't understand why everyone is acting like GNU/Linux has suddenly adopted some closed, non-free element into their system. And it's not as if GNU/Linux has always adhered to this "Unix philosophy" of simple, discreet elements like anti-systemd people seem to think; GNU isn't Unix.

systemd is a nice, simple (to use), and effective system of basic system management and is a welcome relief after the nightmare of years of various init systems that make system administration a headache at its worse.

If you're anti-systemd, you probably don't understand it. If you would take a few steps back and really understand what systemd is, what it does, and how it benefits EVERYONE using GNU/Linux, you'd hopefully agree. I've been using GNU/Linux since the mid-90s (and some of it, professionally) and this is one of the best things that's ever happened to it.

You're certainly free to use other options, since that's what GNU/Linux is about. But don't dismiss systemd just because you don't understand it.

And I don't have your issues of stability/performance; in fact, systemd has been more stable than any init system I've ever had the displeasure of dealing with.

Black box or no (jury's out on that for me, frankly), I don't care to relearn all the very easy to use commands that I prefer from sysv.

Let's say I want to restart the dhcp server.

sysv version:

service isc-dhcp-server start (tab completed, so actually less typing)

Gives me a nice little response:

[ ok ] Starting ISC DHCP server: dhcpd. (The OK is green, so I know everything is good)

systemd version:

systemctl start dhcpd.service

Zero response, so then you have to do:

systemctl status dhcpd.service

an entirely extra step. No nice little colored response. Plus I had to learn the commands that have been working perfectly for 20 years are gone. Oh, and side note, the logs are binary crap. Totally unacceptable. If I wanted to use Redhat, I'd use Redhat. But I don't want to use Redhat. I want to use Debian. Because it used to not suck in this way. But now it does. systemd version: systemctl start dhcpd

The developed countries will become "over-developed" and begin dying of all of the complications that come with lack of movement and excess fat. We are having less children, we are overworked, we are overfed, and we have too much convenience, choice and "luxury" not to move around anymore.

Our lifestyles have become off-kilter and the human body is not designed to keep up with these changes. Perhaps we will in fact go back to "survival of the fittest."
